Annotated parameter values

Source: R/pipeflow.R
pip_param_value.Rd

pip_param_value() is an extension point for handling non-trivial parameter values (e.g. values with units or labels, or parameter objects that carry UI metadata) as step parameters. It can be thought of as a hook that allows you to preprocess or unwrap parameter values before they are passed to the step function. When a step runs, the generic is applied to each unbound argument of the step, that is, to the values that come from params or from the defaults of the step function, and its result is what the step function receives. The stored parameters are not changed, and a method should not change them either: it is called with the stored value, so a method that modifies a reference-backed x such as an environment or an R6 object in place changes the step's parameter on every run.

Usage

pip_param_value(x, ...)

pip_param_value(x, ...) <- value

Arguments

x

The parameter value as stored in the step.

...

Currently unused, reserved for future extensions. Methods should accept it.

value

The plain value to set into the stored value x.

Value

The value the step function receives for the argument.

Details

The default method returns x unchanged. Methods are meant for your own classes, not for base classes such as numeric or character. Note that this is a hook that unwraps a stored value, not an accessor: use pip_get_params() to read parameters from a pipeline.

The generic is not applied to the outputs of other steps (arguments defined as ~step), to partitions or to failure objects. An error in a method is an error of the step and is handled like any other step error, including pip_run(on_error = "continue").

`pip_param_value<-`() is the write side of the same extension point. It turns a plain value into the value that is stored in the step, so that pip_set_params() can keep the annotations of a stored object when it is given a plain value. Dispatch is on x, the value as it is currently stored, and value is the requested value. The default method just returns value. A method decides what a plain value and what an object of its own class means, for example whether to merge it into the stored object or to use it as is.

Like pip_param_value(), this is a hook, not an accessor: x is a stored value, and the parameters of a pipeline are changed with pip_set_params(). The two sides belong together, so that applying pip_param_value() to the result of the setter gives back the plain value that was set:

pip_param_value(`pip_param_value<-`(x, value = v))   # v

pip_set_params() computes the stored value of every affected step before it changes any parameters in the pipeline. If one or more methods fail, an error of class pipeflow_set_params_error reports all failures. This two-phase approach ensures that either all parameter changes are applied successfully or, in case of an error, the pipeline stays unchanged. For that to hold, a method should not modify x in place as this would change pipeline parameters directly. A reference-backed x such as an environment or an R6 object therefore should be copied first.

See also

pip_set_params(), pip_output_value(), pip_run()

Examples

# A value that carries annotations
my_number <- structure(
    list(value = 1.23, label = "Number", descr = "I am an example"),
    class = "foo"
)

# Step functions then simply see the plain value
pip_param_value.foo <- function(x, ...) x$value
registerS3method("pip_param_value", "foo", pip_param_value.foo)

p <- pip_new() |>
    pip_add("double", \(x = 1) x * 2)
pip_set_params(p, list(x = my_number))
pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
pip_collect(p)
#> $double
#> [1] 2.46
#> 

# The write side keeps the annotations when a plain value is set
`pip_param_value<-.foo` <- function(x, ..., value) {
    if (inherits(value, "foo")) {
        return(value)
    }
    x$value <- value
    x
}
registerS3method("pip_param_value<-", "foo", `pip_param_value<-.foo`)

pip_set_params(p, list(x = 42))
pip_get_params(p) # still a "foo" object, now holding 42
#> $x
#> $value
#> [1] 42
#> 
#> $label
#> [1] "Number"
#> 
#> $descr
#> [1] "I am an example"
#> 
#> attr(,"class")
#> [1] "foo"
#> 
pip_run(p, lgr = NULL)
pip_collect(p)
#> $double
#> [1] 84
#>
